statement: Ferrara, Silvia, et al. ("The invention of writing on Rapa Nui (Easter Island). New radiocarbon dates on the Rongorongo script," Scientific Reports 14, 2 Feb 2024, article 53063-7) radiocarbon-dated four rongorongo tablets in a Rome collection: three to the 18th-19th centuries (post-contact), one to 1493-1509 CE — over 200 years before Roggeveen's 1722 European arrival. The authors themselves state the dates "do not allow [researchers] to reach any incontrovertible conclusion" given the "old wood" problem (dated felling, not inscribing) and a sample size of one pre-contact date. Rongorongo's glyph forms don't resemble any known European or other script and have closest formal parallels in Rapa Nui's own rock-carving tradition (circumstantial support for indigenous origin); conversely, no expedition report before Eyraud's 1864 arrival mentions a writing system on the island despite earlier European visits, including a 1770 Spanish annexation ceremony where islanders reportedly witnessed officials "signing" a document (a plausible stimulus-diffusion trigger point). The dating question is genuinely unresolved even in the most recent (2024) primary literature.
scholarly_disagreement: Even the 2024 primary radiocarbon study's own authors decline to resolve pre- vs. post-contact origin from their single early date.

sources.citation: Ferrara, Silvia, et al. "The invention of writing on Rapa Nui (Easter Island). New radiocarbon dates on the Rongorongo script." Scientific Reports 14, 2 Feb 2024, article 53063-7. PMID 38307972.
sources.author: Ferrara et al.

interpretations.position: Rongorongo plausibly predates European contact and represents an independent local invention

holders.name: Ferrara et al., interpreting their own 1493-1509 CE date cautiously

interpretations.strongest_case: One tablet's wood radiocarbon-dated to 1493-1509 CE, over 200 years before Roggeveen's 1722 arrival; glyph forms resemble no known outside script and parallel Rapa Nui's own petroglyph tradition.

interpretations.position: Rongorongo more likely emerged after European contact, stimulated by witnessing literacy

holders.name: Position inferable from the documented absence of any pre-1864 European report of writing on the island, per the surveyed literature

interpretations.strongest_case: No expedition report before Eyraud's 1864 arrival mentions a writing system, despite earlier visits including an 1770 Spanish annexation ceremony where islanders reportedly witnessed officials signing a document; the "old wood" problem means the single early radiocarbon date does not establish inscription date.

does_not_demonstrate: That rongorongo is confirmed pre-contact/independent (the study's own authors decline this conclusion from a single dated specimen)
